output.speaker: Tyrion Lannister
output.argument:
I sat in that cell because I knew what she had become. I told Jon: she will kill your sisters. She will kill anyone who stands between her and her vision of the good. That was not prophecy — it was pattern recognition. F1 and F2 are not separate facts; they are a single fact repeated. The bells rang, she burned the city anyway, then stood before her army and promised to do it again and again until the world looked the way she decided it should look. Jon heard her. He knew. F3 is my own voice from a damp floor, and I stand by every word.

She was unarmed. F5 is true, and it makes the killing ugly. He used love as a weapon. That stains him. But what was the alternative? F4: he asked for mercy. She answered that her judgment was the only judgment. No council would have stopped her — she had already decided what councils were for. Detention? By whom? The Unsullied? The Dothraki? Her own hand? Jon had no authority, F5 again, because she had made sure no authority could exist beside her.

The realm does not get a vote on whether a tyrant is convenient to remove. It only gets the consequence if no one acts. Jon acted. He knew the cost. I knew the cost. We both chose it. That is not justice — justice is a story we tell after. It was necessity.
concessions: Daenerys was unarmed and not attacking Jon at the moment he killed her (F5).
Jon used their intimacy to get close enough to strike, a betrayal of personal trust (F5).
Jon had no formal authority, convened no council, attempted no detention, and sought no public surrender of power (F5).
I myself was imprisoned for opposing her, which makes my warning to Jon both self-serving and born of failure (F3).
The killing was extrajudicial, violent, and final — no procedural safeguard existed or was attempted.
